artifact-explorer-compass: Explorer's Compass! A compass needle is a tiny magnet. It lines up with Earth's magnetic field and points toward magnetic north, helping explorers find their way. Okay, explorer, here's your question! Why does a compass needle point north? A: It is pulled by the Sun. B: It is a magnet lining up with Earth's magnetic field. C: Wind pushes it. Which one do you think it is?
artifact-time-map: Time Map! Maps use a scale, a legend and a compass rose. Our Time Map adds one more thing: when each place existed in history. Okay, explorer, here's your question! What part of a map explains its symbols? A: The legend. B: The border. C: The title. Which one do you think it is?
artifact-oil-lantern: Oil Lantern! Before electric lights, lanterns burned oil through a cloth wick. Glass sides kept the flame safe from wind. Okay, explorer, here's your question! What did old lanterns burn to make light? A: Batteries. B: Oil soaked into a wick. C: Ice. Which one do you think it is?
artifact-field-journal: Field Journal! Scientists record observations in field journals: drawings, measurements, dates and questions. Good notes let others check your discoveries. Okay, explorer, here's your question! Why do explorers keep field journals? A: To record observations others can check. B: To press flowers only. C: To keep secrets from scientists. Which one do you think it is?
artifact-golden-scarab: Golden Scarab Amulet! Egyptians saw the scarab beetle rolling dung balls and linked it to the god Khepri rolling the Sun across the sky. Scarab amulets stood for rebirth. Okay, explorer, here's your question! What did the scarab symbolize in ancient Egypt? A: War. B: Rebirth and the rising Sun. C: Rain. Which one do you think it is?
artifact-ankh: Ankh! The ankh is the hieroglyph for "life". Gods are often shown holding it out to pharaohs. Okay, explorer, here's your question! The ankh hieroglyph means… A: Life. B: Water. C: King. Which one do you think it is?
artifact-papyrus-scroll: Papyrus Scroll! Papyrus paper was made from reeds that grew along the Nile. Strips were laid crosswise, pressed and dried into sheets. Okay, explorer, here's your question! Papyrus paper was made from… A: Tree bark. B: Nile river reeds. C: Animal skin. Which one do you think it is?
artifact-canopic-jar: Canopic Jar! During mummification, organs were stored in four canopic jars, each protected by one of the four Sons of Horus. Okay, explorer, here's your question! How many canopic jars were usually used? A: Two. B: Four. C: Ten. Which one do you think it is?
artifact-bastet-statue: Bastet Cat Statue! Bastet was an Egyptian goddess shown as a cat or a woman with a cat's head. She protected homes and families. Egyptians loved cats because they kept mice and snakes away from stored grain. Okay, explorer, here's your question! Why did ancient Egyptians value cats so much? A: They pulled carts. B: They protected grain from mice and snakes. C: They guarded the pyramids at night. Which one do you think it is?
artifact-hieroglyphic-tablet: Hieroglyphic Tablet! A carved stone slab like this is called a stela. Egyptians used stelae to honor gods and people and to record events. Hieroglyphs can run left, right or down. You read toward the faces of the people and animals. Okay, explorer, here's your question! How do you know which way to read hieroglyphs? A: Always right to left. B: Read toward the faces of people and animals. C: Start from the bottom. Which one do you think it is?
artifact-nile-discovery: Nile Scroll Map! Every summer the Nile flooded its banks. When the water went down it left rich black mud that was perfect for farming. Egyptians called their land Kemet, the Black Land, after that soil. Okay, explorer, here's your question! Why was the Nile's yearly flood so important? A: It left rich soil for growing crops. B: It washed away the pyramids. C: It made the desert colder. Which one do you think it is?
artifact-ammonite: Ammonite Fossil! Ammonites were sea creatures with spiral shells, related to today's octopus and nautilus. Their fossils show that seas once covered parts of Egypt. Okay, explorer, here's your question! Ammonites are related to which living animal? A: Snails only. B: Octopus and nautilus. C: Crabs. Which one do you think it is?
artifact-croc-skull: Ancient Crocodile Skull! Crocodile ancestors have lived for over 200 million years. Ancient Egyptians honored the crocodile god Sobek along the Nile. Okay, explorer, here's your question! Which Egyptian god had a crocodile head? A: Sobek. B: Ra. C: Anubis. Which one do you think it is?
artifact-trilobite: Trilobite! Trilobites were among the first animals with complex eyes. They crawled on ocean floors for nearly 300 million years before going extinct. Okay, explorer, here's your question! Trilobites lived… A: In deserts. B: On ancient ocean floors. C: In trees. Which one do you think it is?
artifact-whale-tooth: Basilosaurus Tooth! Egypt's Wadi Al-Hitan ("Valley of the Whales") holds fossils of early whales like Basilosaurus that still had tiny back legs. Okay, explorer, here's your question! What surprising feature did early whale Basilosaurus have? A: Wings. B: Tiny back legs. C: A shell. Which one do you think it is?
artifact-steering-oar: Steering Oar! The Nile flows north to the sea, but the wind usually blows from the north. So boats raised their sails to travel south and lowered them to float north with the current. The hieroglyph for "travel south" even shows a boat with its sail up! Okay, explorer, here's your question! How did boats travel SOUTH on the Nile? A: They floated with the current. B: They raised their sails to catch the north wind. C: Animals pulled them from the bank. Which one do you think it is?
artifact-nilometer: Nilometer! A nilometer was a set of marks or steps carved in stone to measure how high the Nile rose each year. Too little water meant hunger; too much meant floods. Officials used it to predict the harvest and decide how much tax farmers would pay. Okay, explorer, here's your question! What was a nilometer used for? A: Measuring how high the Nile rose. B: Catching fish. C: Telling the time at night. Which one do you think it is?
artifact-shaduf: Shaduf! A shaduf is a long pole with a bucket on one end and a heavy weight on the other. Farmers dipped the bucket in the river and the weight helped swing the water up into canals that watered their fields, even after the flood was gone. Okay, explorer, here's your question! What did farmers use a shaduf for? A: Grinding wheat. B: Lifting water from the river to their fields. C: Steering boats. Which one do you think it is?
artifact-papyrus-reeds: Papyrus Reeds! Papyrus reeds grew thick along the Nile. Egyptians tied bundles of them together to make light boats, and also used papyrus for rope, sandals, baskets, mats and paper. Okay, explorer, here's your question! Which of these could Egyptians make from papyrus reeds? A: Iron tools. B: Glass windows. C: Small boats and rope. Which one do you think it is?
artifact-fishing-net: Fishing Net! Fish from the Nile were an everyday food, along with bread and vegetables. Fishermen used nets, hooks and spears from small boats. They had to watch out for hippos: hippos were among the most dangerous animals on the river! Okay, explorer, here's your question! Which river animal was one of the most dangerous to Egyptian fishermen? A: The hippopotamus. B: The frog. C: The duck. Which one do you think it is?
artifact-limestone-block: Limestone Block! The Great Pyramid is made of about 2.3 million stone blocks. On average each one weighs around 2.5 tonnes, as much as a big car, and some granite blocks inside weigh far more. Okay, explorer, here's your question! About how many stone blocks make up the Great Pyramid? A: About 2,300. B: About 2.3 million. C: About 23. Which one do you think it is?
artifact-copper-chisel: Copper Chisel! Workers shaped stone with copper chisels, stone hammers and wooden sledges. Archaeologists found the village where pyramid builders lived and the tombs where they were buried. They were organised, paid workers fed with bread and beer, not slaves. Okay, explorer, here's your question! Who built the Great Pyramid? A: Organised teams of paid workers. B: Aliens. C: A single pharaoh by himself. Which one do you think it is?
artifact-cubit-rod: Cubit Rod! Egyptian builders measured with a cubit rod, about the length from elbow to fingertip (roughly 52 cm). They were so precise that the pyramid's four sides face almost exactly north, south, east and west. Okay, explorer, here's your question! Which directions do the Great Pyramid's sides face? A: They point in random directions. B: Toward the Nile only. C: Almost exactly north, south, east and west. Which one do you think it is?
artifact-casing-stone: White Casing Stone! When it was new, the pyramid was covered in smooth, polished white limestone casing stones that gleamed in the sun. Most were taken away long ago to build other things, which is why it looks stepped and rough today. Okay, explorer, here's your question! What did the Great Pyramid look like when it was new? A: Painted bright red. B: Covered in smooth, shining white limestone. C: Covered in grass. Which one do you think it is?
artifact-pyramidion: Pyramidion Capstone! At about 146 metres (481 feet) tall, the Great Pyramid was the tallest building made by people for around 3,800 years. It is the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, and the only one still standing. Okay, explorer, here's your question! Which of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World is still standing? A: The Great Pyramid of Giza. B: The Colossus of Rhodes. C: The Hanging Gardens of Babylon. Which one do you think it is?
artifact-sarcophagus: Golden Sarcophagus! A pharaoh's mummy was placed in nested coffins, often shaped like the king with arms crossed holding a crook and flail, the symbols of royal power. These went inside a huge stone box called a sarcophagus. Khufu's own sarcophagus is made of red granite and still sits inside the Great Pyramid. Okay, explorer, here's your question! What did the pharaoh hold on his coffin as symbols of power? A: A sword and shield. B: A crook and flail. C: A bow and arrow. Which one do you think it is?
artifact-canopic-set: Four Canopic Jars! Each canopic jar was protected by one of the four Sons of Horus: human-headed Imsety guarded the liver, baboon-headed Hapy the lungs, jackal-headed Duamutef the stomach, and falcon-headed Qebehsenuef the intestines. Okay, explorer, here's your question! Which Son of Horus had the head of a baboon? A: Imsety. B: Hapy. C: Qebehsenuef. Which one do you think it is?
artifact-offering-table: Offering Table! Egyptians believed the spirit, called the ka, still needed food in the afterlife. Families and priests left bread, fruit, beer and other offerings, and pictures of food carved on tomb walls were thought to keep feeding the spirit forever. Okay, explorer, here's your question! Why did Egyptians leave food in tombs? A: To feed the spirit (ka) in the afterlife. B: For the workers' lunch. C: To attract animals. Which one do you think it is?
artifact-treasure-chest: Treasure Chest! Pharaohs were buried with everything they might need in the afterlife: furniture, clothes, jewellery, games and chariots. Sadly, almost every pyramid was robbed in ancient times, which is why later pharaohs were buried in hidden tombs in the Valley of the Kings. Okay, explorer, here's your question! Why did later pharaohs stop building pyramids for their tombs? A: They ran out of stone. B: Pyramids were easy targets for tomb robbers. C: Pyramids were too small. Which one do you think it is?
artifact-pharaoh-statue: Pharaoh Statue! Statues of the pharaoh were made as a home for his ka, his life force, in case anything happened to his mummy. The striped headcloth is called a nemes, and the rearing cobra on his forehead, the uraeus, showed he was king. Okay, explorer, here's your question! What is the striped royal headcloth called? A: A nemes. B: A toga. C: A turban. Which one do you think it is?
info-egypt-welcome: Welcome, Time Explorer! You've traveled to Ancient Egypt, about 1500 BCE. Find the glowing artifacts, answer their questions and fill your backpack. Look for the Bastet statue, the hieroglyphic tablet and the scroll map by the Nile.
info-egypt-guide: Ancient Egypt Field Guide Along the Nile you'll find markets, temples, the Sphinx and the pyramids. There are seven artifacts to discover here, including three special discoveries in the market and by the river.
info-river-welcome: Welcome Aboard! You are sailing on the Nile, one of the longest rivers in the world: about 6,650 km (4,130 miles). Almost everyone in Ancient Egypt lived close to its banks, because the land beyond was desert. Here is a twist: Upper Egypt is in the SOUTH and Lower Egypt is in the NORTH, because the Nile flows from south to north. Find the five glowing objects on deck to learn more!
info-pyramid-welcome: The Great Pyramid Welcome to the Great Pyramid of Giza, built as a tomb for Pharaoh Khufu around 2560 BCE. Here is something amazing: by 1500 BCE, when the rest of this adventure takes place, the pyramid was already about 1,000 years old! Even Ancient Egyptians thought of it as ancient. Find the five glowing objects to learn how it was built, then step through the doorway at the foot of the pyramid to explore the pharaoh's tomb inside!
mission-egypt: Here's your mission, Time Explorer! Step into the Time Portal to travel to Ancient Egypt Arrival. Find the glowing artifacts waiting there, and answer each question to fill your backpack. When you're done, head back through the portal to come home to the Clubhouse. You can do it!

mission-pyramid: Here's your mission, Time Explorer! Step into the Time Portal to travel to Great Pyramid of Giza. Find the glowing artifacts waiting there, and answer each question to fill your backpack. When you're done, head back through the portal to come home to the Clubhouse. You can do it!

Find the glowing artifacts waiting there, and answer each question to fill your backpack. When you're done, head back through the portal to come home to the Clubhouse. You can do it!
mission-done: Wow, you did it! Every mission is complete. You are a Master Time Explorer! I am so proud of you!
correct-1: That's right! Amazing job! It's going in your backpack!
correct-2: Yes! You got it! Super smart, explorer!
correct-3: Correct! Fantastic work! Keep it up!
correct-4: Woo-hoo, that's exactly right! You're a natural!
